item.title: ICE Arrests Surge at Airports, Opening New Front in Deportation Drive
item.description:
The Trump administration has begun arresting foreign citizens with expired U.S. visas as they travel through airports, including spouses of Americans, according to documents obtained by The New York Times and interviews with immigration lawyers — a tactic that opens up a vast new pool of people for deportation.

Immigration agents in plain clothes have whisked away targets at check-in counters and arrival gates, with enforcement actions in at least 15 airports in recent weeks. Some of the arrests have occurred quietly, while others have happened as angry fellow passengers filmed the encounters.

The recent arrests appear to be an expansion of an arrangement between the Transportation Security Administration and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The Times reported in December that ICE officers were arresting people with deportation orders at airports with the help of information provided by airlines to the T.S.A.

Now, through a review of Homeland Security Department documents and interviews with lawyers for more than 25 people from more than a dozen countries recently detained at airports, The Times has learned that the program apparently now includes people with expired visas — a much larger group.

Hundreds of thousands of immigrants and visitors overstay visas each year. Many with expired visas occupy a legal gray area, as they are awaiting visa extensions or green cards and have been issued work permits. Such individuals were not prioritized for deportation in the past unless they had committed crimes, and they were rarely detained while waiting for visa extensions or green cards. But that has changed under President Trump, whose administration has undertaken a campaign of mass deportation and views all visa overstays as illegal.

“This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport,” a spokesperson for the Homeland Security Department said in a statement. The agency did not confirm the expansion of the program.

The department, which oversees ICE, has not disclosed how many people have been detained at airports as overstays under the new initiative. The arrests come during a period in which the White House has pushed ICE for more arrests across the country, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has pledged to turn “up the heat on the streets.” To that end, the administration has set a target of 2,000 immigration arrests a day, roughly double the pace from earlier this year.

Interviews with more than a dozen immigration attorneys, advocacy organizations and an airline employee reveal a broad cross-section of targets: an engineer awaiting a work-visa extension, several newlyweds married to U.S. citizens, and a former au pair.

Footage of encounters between travelers and ICE officers have flooded social media. In one widely circulated video, Chantal Morales Rojas, a 27-year-old from Ecuador, was detained by plainclothes officers as she boarded a Southwest Airlines flight from Denver to Oakland, Calif., on July 20. She had been spending the weekend with the family for whom she had worked as an au pair, according to the family.

When Ms. Morales Rojas scanned her boarding pass, an alarm sounded and the gate agent asked her to wait. Moments later, two plainclothes agents intercepted her in the jetway.

“They said they were going to be respectful, that they would be polite,” Alicia Dantzker, a friend of the family, who was on the same flight and filmed part of the encounter, told The Times in an interview. The video captures the men encircling Ms. Morales Rojas, and then ushering her through a side door and down steps to the tarmac as Ms. Dantzker screams for help.

Also among those detained was a Ugandan woman in a wheelchair who has sickle cell anemia and an active asylum application, according to her lawyer.

In another case, ICE attempted to arrest an Australian citizen who had overstayed his visa at the Las Vegas airport, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The scene was recorded by a bystander whose video of the encounter drew wide attention. Officers let him go “to de-escalate the situation and for officer safety,” but ICE ended up taking him into custody a day later when he tried to board a flight in Los Angeles,the department said in a statement.

“In 38 years practicing immigration law, I had never seen this,” said Charles Kuck, who is based in Atlanta and is representing an Indian engineer who was detained while awaiting a work-permit extension. “And I know it’s happening to lots of people.”

Shannon Shepherd, an immigration lawyer who is vice chair for the Chicago chapter of the American Immigration Lawyers Association, said she and other lawyers were revising longstanding advice about domestic air travel.

“Before, I was saying, ‘As long as you have an ID, you can travel domestically,’” Ms. Shepherd said. “Now I am turning around and saying, ‘If you are in the process of changing status, avoid any travel.’”

The original collaboration between T.S.A. and ICE began in May 2025, when the airport security agency started sharing information with the immigration agency for enforcement purposes, according to a document obtained via the Freedom of Information Act from the government transparency group American Oversight and shared with The Times.

ICE shared names of individuals with deportation orders with the airport agency, which would run them through its databases and report any hits to ICE for potential arrest. It was a remarkable shift from past practices, when the federal government avoided involving the T.S.A. in immigration enforcement for fear of disrupting domestic travel.

Now, “the net they are casting for people they want to detain is far wider,” said Ghassan Shamieh, an immigration lawyer in San Francisco.

“It’s not people with criminal records” being targeted, Mr. Shamieh said. “You are talking about people with legitimate pending applications.”

Mr. Shamieh has four clients who were detained at airports in the last 10 days, including two women who recently married Americans and are in the process of obtaining permanent residency through their spouses. One of the husbands was with his wife when she was taken into custody after they landed in Burbank, Calif.

On Tuesday morning, an immigration judge granted her release on a $35,000 bond. But D.H.S. lawyers reserved the right to appeal within 30 days, and she is likely to remain detained until they decide.

Ms. Morales Rojas, the au pair, entered the United States lawfully in January 2023 as a J-1 exchange visitor, a legal status that allowed her to work for two years, according to her lawyer. Her visa expired Jan. 4, 2025, according to D.H.S. Before the exchange program ended, Ms. Morales Rojas filed an application with immigration authorities to remain in the country, said the lawyer, Laura Lichter.

“During the last three and a half years, Morales Rojas lived openly in the United States with the government’s knowledge of her pending case, passed repeated background checks, and received work authorization from D.H.S. while waiting for her application to be reviewed,” Ms. Lichter said. “The process she’s pursuing is completely lawful.”

But homeland security officials said in a statement that “in violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her visa.” On Tuesday afternoon, a judge granted her release on a $3,000 bond, and she is likely to leave detention by Wednesday.

Ms. Lichter has filed suit challenging the government’s decision to arrest and detain Ms. Morales Rojas without a proper arrest warrant and without an individualized determination that detention was necessary.

Lauren and Scott Cahr, her former employers, said they had hired Ms. Morales Rojas when their first child, Silas, was 6 months old. The Cahrs said in an interview that they had flown Ms. Morales Rojas to Denver during an Ultimate Frisbee tournament that they attended, and she had helped care for Silas and his little brother.

The family formed a deep bond, and the Cahrs created a custom photo book titled “The Adventures of Chanty and Gordo,” the nicknames Ms. Morales Rojas and their son called each other, as a parting gift.

“She is an amazing young woman who we were so lucky to have in our lives,” Ms. Cahr said. “We have tried to maintain a consistent relationship with her.”

Ms. Cahr has visited Ms. Morales Rojas in detention, while members of the Cahrs’ Ultimate Frisbee community have launched a GoFundMe campaign to help cover legal costs.

item.title: Georgia Teen Is Sentenced to Life for Deadly School Shooting
item.description:
A Georgia teenager was sentenced on Tuesday to life in prison for carrying out an attack at his high school that killed two students and two teachers and left a trail of grief in a suburban community near Atlanta.

A judge decided that the boy, Colt Gray, now 16, should spend the rest of his life in prison without the possibility of parole. He had pleaded guilty last week to 55 charges, including murder and aggravated assault, in connection with the 2024 shooting at Apalachee High School in Winder, Ga. He was 14 at the time and beginning his freshman year.

The guilty plea spared Winder, a small city northeast of Atlanta, the inherent uncertainty of a trial. But the sentencing hearing itself spanned days. Agonizing victim impact statements and other testimony excavated the panic and anguish in the hours after the shooting, the fitful path toward recovery for survivors and the families of those killed, and the downward spiral of an adolescent who had access to a rifle but not the psychological support he urgently needed.

At the start of the hearing, Judge Nicholas Primm of Barrow County Superior Court said his discretion was limited: By statute, Mr. Gray would receive a life sentence, but it was up to the judge to determine whether Mr. Gray would ever be eligible for parole.

On Tuesday, Judge Primm said that he had weighed Mr. Gray’s age and immaturity, as well as his acceptance of his guilt, against the depravity of the attack. His crimes, done in pursuit of infamy, the judge said, placed Mr. Gray in “an irredeemable moral wasteland.”

“You understood the horror of what you were going to do,” Judge Primm said. “You wrote, ‘I want to make history. I want people to remember the pain I caused.’ And there you succeeded — the pain that you visited upon this community is unlikely to disappear in my lifetime.”

As the judge spoke, Mr. Gray did not react. But family members of victims, survivors and others sighed with a measure of relief, cried and embraced as soon as the judge said Mr. Gray should never be released from prison.

Mr. Gray had been scheduled to go on trial in October, but the change in plea had been anticipated, especially given that his father had been convicted in March of murder and involuntary manslaughter, among other charges.

The shooting — the deadliest school shooting in Georgia history — attracted national attention because prosecutors succeeded in holding his father criminally responsible for the attack. Prosecutors pointed to his allowing his son virtually unfettered access to the weapon used in the attack — a rifle given as a Christmas gift — and failing to heed signs of his son’s deteriorating mental health.

The father’s sentencing hearing is scheduled to begin on Thursday.

During the father’s trial and in the recent sentencing testimony, prosecutors presented a series of witnesses and evidence that portrayed the shooting on Sept. 4, 2024, as the culmination of years of escalating family turmoil and a growing obsession with violence for the younger Mr. Gray.

Well before the shooting, Mr. Gray would have violent outbursts and flashes of overwhelming anxiety, family members testified. He told them that he’d hear voices urging him to act aggressively.

Mental health experts said he had been affected by the persistent isolation and neglect of his childhood. But they also said he was malingering and that the symptoms he described seemed exaggerated or highly improbable, like hearing voices only on specific days of the week. They testified that they believed he did not have schizophrenia or bipolar disorder.

In a search of his home immediately after the shooting, investigators found a collage on his bedroom wall of photographs of the 19-year-old perpetrator of the attack at a high school in Parkland, Fla., in 2018 and news clippings related to that shooting, in which 17 people were killed.

He had also left detailed plans. In the sentencing hearing, prosecutors showed stick-figure drawings Mr. Gray had made in a notebook, apparently mimicking sketches by the Parkland gunman.

Prosecutors shared recordings from phone calls with his mother from jail in which Mr. Gray relished the notoriety he had gained from the attack. “I’m in the big leagues, bro,” he told his mother, at one point comparing himself to the man who attempted to assassinate President Trump in 2024.

Still, his maternal grandmother, Deborah Polhamus, testified that she had seen some improvements while he was in jail. He had a routine and psychological treatment and medication — things, she said, he did not have before.

“He’s thriving,” Ms. Polhamus said. “He’s more like the Colt I saw growing up.”

In the years before the shooting, Mr. Gray had spent much of his childhood jostled by turbulence. He enrolled in seven schools over four years, as his family bounced between homes, sometimes because of eviction. His mother struggled with substance abuse and legal troubles. His family eventually split, with his younger sisters living with their mother and him with his father, until his father gained sole custody of all three.

When Mr. Gray was in middle school and living in a nearby county, sheriff’s deputies visited the boy’s home after the F.B.I. traced an anonymous threat about a school shooting made on an online message board to his address. But the investigation was dropped after the boy could not be definitively connected to the posts.

In 2024, after missing his eighth-grade year entirely, Mr. Gray entered Apalachee as a freshman. There, he attended class only occasionally; Sept. 4, already several weeks into the academic year, was Mr. Gray’s fifth school day.

In the sentencing hearing, some survivors, like Natalie Griffith, conjured alternative scenarios imagining if Mr. Gray had held off. Maybe, she said, he would have found a place for himself on campus and found friends. “If you had just waited,” said Ms. Griffith, a student at Apalachee.

She also would not have gone through painful surgeries and physical therapy to try to regain the full use of her hand. “I wonder if the person I am today,” she said, “is the person I would have been if the shooting had not occurred.”

Jessica Rehberg, the principal, described the chaos caused by the shooting. “He turned staff members into impromptu paramedics and caregivers,” she recalled. And she described the lasting consequences beyond the stolen lives and major physical injuries, like the hundreds of students whose ability to learn was disrupted long after the shooting was over.

“He destroyed what once felt like the most safe and secure place,” Ms. Rehberg said. “He stole the ability to focus and not zone out. He turned conversations about ‘Where should we eat after the football game?’ into ‘Is it even safe enough to go?’”

Because of that, she told the judge, “he deserves the harshest consequences.”

Standing in the courtroom, some saw an opportunity to speak directly to Mr. Gray, as he sat just a few feet away. They sought to convey the fury and the grief they blame him for.

“I’m angry at how cowardly you are,” Alanna Wallace, the sister of Mason Schermerhorn, a 14-year-old student who was killed, said in court.

She described the videos and photographs she has seen from that day at Apalachee — harrowing images burned into her mind.

“You saw him scared and running,” Ms. Wallace said. “And then you proceeded to shoot him in the head.”

item.title: Obama to Headline Democratic Redistricting Fund-Raiser
item.description:
Former President Barack Obama will hold a fund-raiser in late August for the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, a fresh sign that Democrats intend to continue their aggressive push to gerrymander congressional districts ahead of the 2028 election.

The fund-raiser will take place on Martha’s Vineyard and will be hosted by Eric Holder, the former attorney general under Mr. Obama and the chairman of the committee, which is the main Democratic group focused on redistricting.

While Democrats appear to have exhausted all of their options for new maps before the midterm elections this year, their focus on the 2028 election still requires investment in crucial, state-level elections this fall. Democrats hope to protect or build trifectas in various states — single-party control of both chambers of legislatures plus the governor’s office — or Democratic supermajorities that would allow them to override a hostile governor’s veto.

The emergence of Mr. Obama on the political fund-raising circuit comes as Democrats, at least at the national level, are facing a significant cash shortfall.

Drawing even with Republicans in the national redistricting wars has been a top priority for Mr. Holder, Mr. Obama and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader. Mr. Obama, who remains one of the party’s most popular and influential figures, was a prominent supporter of a congressional gerrymander in California and an attempted one in Virginia.

“The race by Republicans to gerrymander is not over — and between potential redraws and the November election, the 2028 redistricting fight is already underway,” John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Details of the fund-raiser were first reported by Punchbowl News.

Democrats have largely been playing catch-up on the national redistricting front. Ever since President Trump sparked the battle by imploring Republicans in Texas to take the rare partisan step of redrawing their congressional map last year to benefit Republicans in the midterms, Democrats have faced a host of hurdles, largely because of redistricting reforms pushed by Mr. Obama, Mr. Holder and other Democrats.

The result has been the creation of as many as a dozen new districts that will favor Republicans this year.

Democrats have turned their attention to 2028 with the goal of reversing that new advantage and then some. States including New York, Virginia, Illinois and Maryland have all signaled a desire to redraw their maps for the next cycle. California could also try to redraw its map yet again, and some Democrats hope Washington and Oregon will join the battle, as well.

Republicans are also poised to redraw maps in many states in 2028, including Indiana, Mississippi, Nebraska and Kansas — as well as states redrawn in the past year, including Texas, Alabama and Louisiana, where further opportunities may lie.

item.title: Graham and Netanyahu Worked Together to Denounce International Criminal Court
item.description:
Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died this month at 71, worked privately with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel to coordinate a bipartisan group of lawmakers to denounce the International Criminal Court investigation into Mr. Netanyahu just before the 2024 election, footage of their discussions shows.

The conversations were among roughly 400 hours recorded by the British filmmaker Alex Holder, who trailed Mr. Graham for roughly four years for a planned documentary project titled “Lindsey’s Game.” The footage of two discussions with Mr. Netanyahu about rebuking the I.C.C. was reviewed by The New York Times.

The calls took place just days before the 2024 election, on Oct. 29, as Mr. Graham was in Ohio, where he was campaigning with Donald Trump Jr. for Bernie Moreno in a Senate race, according to Mr. Holder.

The discussions underscore the significance of the relationship between Mr. Graham and Mr. Netanyahu and its impact, including with the senator’s colleagues. The two men were days away from an election that would return Donald J. Trump to the White House. Mr. Graham was a valuable interlocutor for Mr. Netanyahu even before that, but the call took place as the prime minister was prepared to discuss with Mr. Trump waging an increasingly expansive war against Iran.

Mr. Netanyahu was in Washington on Tuesday for Mr. Graham’s funeral, as well as a meeting with Mr. Trump about the war in Iran, which is becoming an intractable problem for the president.

Mr. Netanyahu remains the subject of an arrest warrant by the I.C.C., but Israeli officials have called the effort politically motivated. Mr. Netanyahu has made foreign trips since it was issued, and is set to travel to the U.N. General Assembly in New York in September.

Mr. Trump has declared that he will not be arrested, despite Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling Mr. Netanyahu a war criminal and saying he had reviewed whether city officials had the power to make an arrest. The mayor later said officials concluded they did not.

In the first call with Mr. Netanyahu, which was recorded on video, Mr. Graham is seen and heard talking to the prime minister, whose voice is occasionally garbled as it comes through the line and is picked up on the senator’s microphone. But Mr. Netanyahu could be heard clearly as he discussed a pending decision by the I.C.C. about whether to seek his arrest for alleged war crimes, as a prosecutor with the court had recommended earlier in 2024.

“A three-judge panel,” Mr. Netanyahu said in the first call with Mr. Graham, will be “making the decision very soon.” He noted that the court’s chief prosecutor, Karim A. A. Khan, had faced allegations of sexual misconduct, and suggested to Mr. Graham that “the great cloud that it shed” could help delay the arrest warrant (Mr. Khan was removed from his position last week, the court’s oversight body announced.)

“It is possible to have to appeal to the court to say, ‘OK, we want to review this before you do anything, before you issue an arrest warrant. There has to be a review about this entire process,’” Mr. Netanyahu said, adding that “this cloud or this stain has to be removed” before moving forward.

“And I suggest that you send a letter, with, maybe some other senators,”Mr. Netanyahu said. When Mr. Graham offered up Speaker Mike Johnson as the “perfect person” to sign such a letter, Mr. Netanyahu replied, “Would he get Democrats?”

Mr. Graham said that he would try for a bipartisan approach.

Mr. Holder recorded the audio, without video, of a second call between the two men that he said took place later that day. Only Mr. Graham’s voice could be heard.

On that call, Mr. Graham joked to Mr. Netanyahu that he should “pay me for all this. I should get tons of shekels.” It would take “more than dinner,” he added.

He then said that “we got them both,” appearing to refer to Senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ben Cardin of Maryland, two Democrats, who said they would sign a letter protesting the efforts to move ahead with an arrest warrant.

“So here’s why I’m calling you,” Mr. Graham told Mr. Netanyahu, saying he hoped to get the letter “out the door Wednesday,” appearing to refer to the next day, October 30. “So send me over whatever you want to say. And they want to say two things” to the I.C.C.

One was that the prosecutors should speak with the Israeli government and not move ahead with the case until “the cloud is lifted” from the prosecutor’s own problems.

What Mr. Graham requested in exchange, he said, was for Mr. Netanyahu “to call Blumenthal and Cardin and thank them for being fair-minded on this, and also thank them for trying to help with Saudi-Israel normalization. You appreciate it. You’re very interested in it, and that will encourage both of them.”

The letter was released on Nov. 1, 2024, and included Mr. Blumenthal and Mr. Cardin as signers. In addition to noting the allegations against Mr. Khan, the letter said that the I.C.C. did “not comply” with the law by declining to keep a planned meeting with Israeli representatives before applying for the arrest warrant.

A spokesman for Mr. Netanyahu did not respond to an email seeking comment on the calls.

Mr. Blumenthal declined to address questions about the calls Mr. Graham had with Mr. Netanyahu. An aide to Mr. Cardin did not respond to an email seeking comment.

item.title: Trump’s Spy Chief Spends Final Hours in Job Boasting of Mass Firings
item.description:
Bill Pulte, the acting director of national intelligence, has spent his final days on the job celebrating his efforts to terminate employees in his office.

But current and former officials said few people have actually been fired in recent weeks from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, despite a flurry of social media posts by Mr. Pulte. And members of Congress have been left scratching their heads about whether Mr. Pulte has cut nearly as many employees as he has claimed.

Mr. Pulte said on Tuesday, hours before the Senate is expected to confirm his replacement, Jay Clayton, that he had reduced the staff at his organization by nearly a third since taking the job of spy chief in June.

“Good News! In addition to the Historic DECLASSIFICATIONS (Transparency!) by the President, we are, this morning, Executing a 5th and Near Final Round of TERMINATIONS, an approximately 30% Staff Reduction from Weeks Ago,” Mr. Pulte wrote in an X post that mimicked President Trump’s social media patois. “The Intelligence Community must protect the American people, NOT the political whims of the bloated and corrupt elite class.”

But Mr. Pulte’s office has provided no details or explanations of the purported cuts, sowing doubts on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Pulte, who also oversees a federal housing agency and has pursued campaigns of retribution against Mr. Trump’s perceived enemies, lacked any national security experience before he was tapped to run the spy office.

“The acting D.N.I. has been quick to announce firings and make public claims about them, but has so far declined to provide the Senate Intelligence Committee with the information necessary to assess the accuracy of those statements or the basis for those decisions,” said Rachel Cohen, a spokeswoman for Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the committee.

Mr. Pulte has not laid out the goals of his purported reductions. A spokeswoman for Mr. Pulte did not respond to questions about his social media posts.

But several former U.S. intelligence officials expressed disbelief about the claim of reductions. They said Mr. Pulte was counting people whose tour of duty at the office was complete and were returning to their home agencies as previously planned. He also appears to be counting unfilled positions at the National Counterterrorism Center and other parts of the spy office as terminations, former officials said.

Still, current and former officials said, the elimination of jobs and returning officers to their home agencies have hit hardest at the National Intelligence Council, a group that reviews the conclusions of a variety of spy agencies.

In many respects, the council is a core part of the spy chief’s office, developing authoritative analytic judgments supported by a variety of intelligence agencies, while guarding against groupthink.

Last year, Tulsi Gabbard, the previous director, fired the head of the council in a dispute over intelligence about a Venezuelan gang. She also eliminated the council’s Strategic Futures Group, arguing its work was at odds with Mr. Trump’s policies.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence had about 1,700 employees when Ms. Gabbard announced in May that she was stepping down, including around 1,300 full-time government employees and 400 contractors.

Mr. Pulte initially put a handful of close aides to Ms. Gabbard on administrative leave, allowing them to find other jobs in the government. He also directed about 75 intelligence officers who formally worked for other spy agencies, like the C.I.A., the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency or others, to return to those agencies.

Julia Curlee, a former longtime C.I.A. analyst who left the agency this year, criticized Mr. Pulte’s efforts to cut intelligence professionals as a performance intended to please Mr. Trump that may have long-term consequences for America’s spy agencies.

“The bill will come due in low morale and in Americans who now won’t apply,” said Ms. Curlee, who served on the White House National Security Council during the first few months of the second Trump administration. “Congress should demand to know what this is meant to achieve, and which national security functions will go unperformed.”

item.title: Senators Forge a Deal on Graham’s Russia Sanctions Bill
item.description:
Senators on Tuesday announced a breakthrough in a long-stalled bipartisan effort to advance sweeping sanctions against Russia, paving the way for an evening test vote on the compromise bill after the Washington funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, its main champion.

Republicans and Democrats said they had addressed concerns from members of both parties and were ready to push ahead in efforts to pass the measure in honor of Mr. Graham, who spent the final hours of his life working in Ukraine to cement it.

The measure would impose harsh new penalties on countries that purchase oil and other energy products from Russia, as well as extend existing sanctions against Iran seeking to limit its ability to fuel its wartime economy.

“We are proud to announce an agreement on legislation to stop purchasers of Russian oil and gas from fueling Putin’s war machine and to continue restricting the Iranian regime’s ability to support terrorism and build its nuclear program,” said a joint statement from the Republican senators Darline Graham of South Carolina, Jim Risch of Idaho, Roger Wicker of Mississippi and Katie Britt of Alabama and the Democratic senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire. “There is no greater way to honor Senator Graham’s legacy than to move forward with this bipartisan agreement, and we look forward to today’s vote.”

The announcement came just as lawmakers and his family gathered at the Capitol to honor Mr. Graham’s life, and hours before the president and world leaders convened at the National Cathedral for his funeral.

An initial vote was expected on Tuesday evening, just after President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has long pressed for such a sanctions package, was to meet with senators on Capitol Hill.

The revised legislation reflects an intense round of negotiations to narrow the measure’s provisions and ensure tighter congressional oversight over the penalties it would impose.

To appease Democrats who had balked at handing President Trump new tariff authority, the revised measure would require that the president impose the sanctions rather than simply permit him to do so — though Mr. Trump could still waive them if he certified that it was necessary for national security reasons. Negotiators also added requirements that the administration regularly report to Congress on how the penalties were being carried out.

Senators also said they had adjusted language governing the bill’s secondary tariffs to exempt American allies that still purchase small amounts of oil, gas and other energy from Russia if they were demonstrably reducing their reliance on Russian-produced energy.

Mr. Blumenthal, who had worked with Mr. Graham on the measure for more than a year, said he was confident the changes would secure enough backing to overcome any objections from Democrats and yield the votes necessary for the measure to move ahead.

“We’ve got a solid core of 60-plus senators,” Mr. Blumenthal said.

item.title: Who Wins (and Who Loses) in the Democrats’ New 2028 Primary Calendar?
item.description:
Democrats across the country agree that their new primary map will redraw the road to their party’s 2028 presidential nomination. But, as they look to what’s widely expected to be a crowded and competitive contest, no one is quite sure what turns it will take.

Instead of Iowa and New Hampshire, long the traditional openers of the primary process, Democratic candidates will navigate their way through a six-state gantlet that starts in South Carolina on Jan. 22, winds through Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico and Michigan and ends in Virginia on Feb. 29.

The cross-country sprint has significantly broadened the race — geographically, racially and ideologically, Democratic strategists say.

“It really could benefit anyone,” said Rob Flaherty, a deputy campaign manager for former Vice President Kamala Harris’s 2024 run and the co-host of “Nobody Knows Anything,” a podcast about national politics. “I follow things pretty closely, and I have no idea how it’s going to bounce.”

Here’s what the calendar does — and doesn’t — tell us about the 2028 Democratic primary race.

The new map is good news for Black voters, increasing their power in the earliest stage of the contest. While the electorate in Iowa and New Hampshire is largely white, a majority of South Carolina Democratic primary voters are Black.

“Black voters are the backbone of this party,” said Christale Spain, the chair of the state’s Democratic Party, in an interview with the political commentator Roland Martin last week. “We should continue to elevate Black voters role in the process.”

Harris, who has floated the possibility of a third presidential run, remains popular with Black voters and could be advantaged by South Carolina’s spot at the head of the line — but it’s hard to predict. In 2020, she exited the race before the state even voted, with her fund-raising having run dry.

Some commentators pointed to the possibility that multiple Black candidates — including perhaps Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland and Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia — could split the electorate, sending the race into the next contests with muddled results.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who has a history of building coalitions with Black voters, could be strong in the state. Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, struggled there in 2020.

The new map more than doubles the share of Latino voters across the first four states from 2020, the last time Democrats had a competitive presidential primary, according to an analysis by Decision Desk HQ, an election results reporting website.

The heavy Latino populations in Nevada and New Mexico give those voters a pivotal role in culling the field as the candidates move through the early contests.

While Latino voters are generally considered more socially moderate, Senator Bernie Sanders, the liberal Vermont independent, won big in Nevada after investing heavily in organizing there in 2020. Working-class Latino voters could also be inclined toward candidates like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona.

“The Black voters are going to kick off the calendar,” said Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist. “But I do think that Latino voters will ultimately decide who the nominee is.”

The announcement of the new calendar prompted grumbles from some corners of the progressive world that the Democratic National Committee had created a schedule designed to hamper insurgent left-wing candidates.

But it’s not clear what kind of candidate is favored by the new calendar.

The six early states are relatively inexpensive to advertise in, which could provide the opportunity for an insurgent to catch fire — though in 2020, South Carolina elevated Joseph R. Biden Jr., an establishment candidate, over Mr. Sanders.

On the other hand, the new map rewards campaigns with the money to build a six-state, cross-country organization that can reach diverse constituencies. That may benefit candidates like Ms. Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who could enter the race with well-established political brands and expansive fund-raising lists.

One of the biggest changes to the calendar is bumping New Hampshire from its vaunted “first in the nation” position.

New Hampshire law requires the state’s presidential primary to be held at least seven days before any “similar election.” That standard would bump its primary into mid-January, before South Carolina.

In past elections, New Hampshire has been immovable. In 2024, party leaders also tried to move the state back in the calendar. It voted first anyhow, risking its delegates in the process.

Local officials have promised to once again defend the state’s tradition. But in 2028, the penalties for candidates could be onerous: The party has threatened to bar any candidate who campaigns in a state that jumps the calendar from participating in official party debates.

That change could hurt Mr. Buttigieg, who has shown strength in the state.

New Hampshire also runs an open primary, allowing independent voters to participate in party contests. That dynamic has made it a place where moderates can gain steam — a benefit such candidates will no longer get.
